A gym with 500 or more members and a year of check-ins means tens of thousands of rows handled about eight times for one tap. On a cheap desk phone this can show as a pause after pressing Save that grows every month. It has not been measured: no speed test runs with a big gym.
expected: A save handles only the rows it changes, so pressing Save takes the same short time on day 1 and in year 3, and a speed test with a 500-member gym proves it.
who: front desk and owners of bigger gyms
how_often: every save from a desk form
fix_line: Run each save on just the member's own rows and time it with a 500-member test gym

title: The member import's code is part of every first download of the admin app
what: The import of members from Excel or CSV (column matching, AI matching, branches, ID scrubbing, saving: about 3,000 lines) is loaded up front with the rest of the admin app, although a gym uses it about once. Only the spreadsheet reader itself is fetched later. Desk staff and trainers on a slow phone connection pay for it on every first open. The admin app has no speed score (it needs a login), so the real seconds are not measured.
expected: The import screen and its rules download only when someone opens Import members.
who: everyone who opens the admin app
how_often: every first open of the admin app
fix_line: Load the import screen only when it is opened, like the spreadsheet reader already is

title: Filling in missing details for members already in the gym saves one member at a time
what: When an owner imports a sheet again and chooses to fill in blank details of existing members, each member is saved separately and the next waits for the last. New members go 500 per save, but these go one by one, so a gym with 500 existing members waits for 500 trips to the server in a row; on a slow phone connection that is minutes with the import screen open.
expected: Existing members' blanks are filled in a few large saves, like new members are, so the import finishes in seconds.
fix_line: Send the fill-in changes in batches instead of one member per save

title: Each mobile number another desk added meanwhile makes the import resend up to 500 rows
what: If a member with the same mobile was added by someone else while the import runs, the whole batch of up to 500 is refused, one row is taken out, and the whole batch is sent again. Several such numbers in one batch mean several full resends.
expected: One refused number costs one small retry, not a full resend of the batch each time.
who: owners importing while the desk adds members
fix_line: Have the server skip mobiles already in the gym and report them, in one pass

title: The owner's numbers on Today go through every member, plan, payment and check-in about 30 times each time they are worked out
what: To draw the small trend lines under 'Fees due' and 'Stopped coming', the Today numbers work out the whole dues list and the whole 'losing the habit' list once for every point on the line: 30 points for the default 30 days, plus one more each for the totals and the day before. Each time it runs through all members, all plans, all receipts and all check-ins again. A gym with 500 or more members has tens of thousands of check-ins a year, so this is dozens of full passes on the owner's phone every time Today opens or the gym's data changes. The opened tile's page does the same work again. Not timed on a real phone.
expected: Each list is gone through once and each day's figure is read from that one pass, so Today opens just as fast for a big gym as for a small one.
who: owners of big gyms on the Today screen
how_often: every time Today opens or the gym's data changes
fix_line: Work out the dues and stopped-coming lines in one pass over the data instead of one pass per day

title: All branches downloads every other branch's whole history each time it is opened
what: When an owner opens the All branches page, the admin app fetches every other branch's full records (all members, plans, receipts and every check-in ever made) from the start, because it keeps no saved copy of the other branches. A gym with three branches of 500+ members and a few years of check-ins waits for several large downloads on a phone on 4G, every visit, before the totals appear.
expected: The other branches open from a saved copy and fetch only what changed, or the server sends just the totals and short lists this page shows.
who: owners with two or more branches
how_often: every time All branches is opened in a new visit
fix_line: Keep a saved copy of each branch and fetch only changes, or ask the server for the page's totals only

title: Each letter typed in the All branches member search re-sorts every branch's whole history
what: The 'Find a member in any branch' box searches again on every key press, and each search re-groups every plan, receipt and check-in of every branch, even though only the matching members are shown. In a big gym with several branches the box can lag on a cheap phone while typing a name or number.
expected: Typing stays instant: the search waits for a short pause and only works out the members that match.
who: owners with two or more branches
how_often: every key press in the search box
fix_line: Build each branch's member list once and filter it; wait for a pause before searching

title: Giving free days to all challenge winners at once sends one request per winner, one after another
what: When the owner taps the button to give (or skip) the prize for every winner of a finished challenge, the panel asks the server for each winner in turn and waits for each answer before the next. On slow 4G that is about a second per winner, so 50 winners keeps the owner waiting close to a minute, and one failed request stops the rest without saying which winners were done.
expected: All winners are handled in one request, or in parallel, and the screen says clearly who got the days and who did not.
who: owners of busy gyms running challenges
fix_line: Send all winners in one server call and report each winner's result

title: The Visits screen goes through the gym's whole check-in history about eight times after every check-in
what: Each check-in at the desk changes the visit list, and the Visits screen then works out again, from every visit the gym ever had, the Losing the habit count, who is in today, the day's register, the 30-day chart, the summary and the busy hours. A gym with 500 members and a few years of check-ins has tens of thousands of visits, so each tap gets slower on a cheap desk phone as the gym ages.
expected: Only the recent days the screen shows are re-counted, and the Losing the habit count is worked out once, not on every check-in.
who: desk staff at big, older gyms
fix_line: Count from the last few weeks of visits only and keep the risk count from refreshing on each tap

title: The day's register, a batch list and the Losing the habit list draw every row at once
what: The search box shows at most 8 matches, but the register of a day, a picked batch and the Losing the habit list have no limit and no Show more. In a 500-member gym a busy day or a long risk list puts hundreds of cards with buttons on the page at once, which scrolls and redraws slowly on a cheap phone.
expected: Long lists show the first part and a Show more, like the member search and the measurement history already do.
who: desk staff and owners of big gyms
fix_line: Show the first 50 rows with a Show more button

title: Each member who leaves makes the database read the leaderboard records of every gym
what: When a member leaves, the clean-up removes their leaderboard days and board line and blanks the phone on their challenge wins. None of the three lists has an index that starts with the member, so each leave reads all of those lists for every gym. The days list grows with every gym and member, so this gets slower as MettleUp grows. The database's own advisor flags two of the three.
expected: Each of the three lists has an index on the member, so a leave touches only that member's rows.
who: every gym, as the platform grows
fix_line: Add an index on the member for the three leaderboard lists

title: The Members list and the Money collections list draw every row at once
what: The Members page puts every member on screen in one go (a card each on a phone, a table row each on a computer), and filters and re-sorts the whole list again on every letter typed in the search box. Money, Collections does the same for every receipt in the chosen dates, so a custom range of a year at a 500-member gym draws thousands of rows. On a cheap desk phone these pages get slow to open and typing in the search lags as the gym grows.
expected: Long lists show the first screenful or a page at a time (or only draw what is on screen), and the search waits for a short pause in typing before it filters.
who: owners and desk staff of bigger gyms
how_often: every time the page opens or a letter is typed
fix_line: Show long lists a page at a time and wait for a pause before searching

title: The Trainers page downloads every trainer's photo again each time the week changes or a session is booked
what: Trainer photos travel inside the week's schedule answer, as text of up to about 140 KB each, instead of as separate pictures the browser can keep. Every move to the next or previous week, every booking, every cancel and every Refresh fetches the whole answer again, photos included. A gym with 8 trainers sends close to a megabyte per tap over slow 4G, and the page waits for it before showing the new week.
expected: Photos are fetched once and kept by the browser; changing the week or booking only fetches the bookings.
who: owners and trainers using the Trainers page
how_often: every week change, booking or cancel
fix_line: Send trainer photos once as pictures and leave them out of the week's bookings read

title: The Shop page shows only the newest 300 orders, so its Collected, Cancelled and All counts stop growing
what: The server hands the admin app only the newest 300 shop orders. The Shop page counts New, Ready, Collected, Cancelled and All from that list, so once a gym passes 300 orders the counts freeze near 300 and older orders disappear from the All tab with no note and no way to see them. A busy gym of 500 members ordering a shake now and then gets there in a few months.
expected: The counts are the real totals, and older orders can still be looked up (a Show older button or a date pick).
who: owners and desk staff of busy shops
how_often: every time, once a gym has over 300 orders
fix_line: Count totals on the server and let the page fetch older orders on request

title: Every open admin screen downloads the newest 300 shop orders again every minute
what: Whatever screen the owner or desk has open, the admin app re-reads the newest 300 shop orders, with every line of each order, once a minute while the tab is in view, only to see whether anything is new. On a desk phone on mobile data this is a steady download all day, most of it orders that have not changed.
expected: The app asks only for orders new or changed since its last look, so an idle minute costs almost nothing.
who: every gym with the member app on
how_often: every minute the admin app is in view
fix_line: Ask the server only for orders changed since the last read

title: The list of members in the app is downloaded whole by three screens on their own, and redrawn the slow way
what: The full list of everyone who joined the gym in the app, with their order counts, has no paging. The Joined in the app list reads it every minute, the Messages page every 2 minutes, and the Today page every 5 minutes for the birthday wish, even when that reminder is off. On the Joined list each row is matched against the gym's whole member list by mobile number, and this is redone on every redraw, at least every 30 seconds: with 500 in the app and 800 on the books that is about 400,000 number clean-ups each time on a cheap desk phone.
expected: One shared copy of the list, read only when needed, and a page of 50 at a time; the mobile-number match is worked out once per change.
who: gyms with many members in the app
how_often: every minute a list screen is open
fix_line: Keep one shared app-member list, page it, and build the mobile lookup once

title: Every app open and every leave re-reads the member's whole workout history for the cloud copy
what: For a member signed in to a MettleUp account, the app reads every workout and every set ever logged, packs and compares them, 3 seconds after each app open and each time the app is left, even when nothing changed. This runs inside the same queue as the app's own saves, so a member who opens the app and starts logging right away waits behind it; with years of history the delay grows with every workout.
expected: The copy only reads what changed since the last copy, so opening the app and starting a workout feels the same on day 1 and in year 3.
who: members signed in to a MettleUp account
how_often: every app open and every time the app is left
fix_line: Drop the forced full read at open and leave when the change stamp is unchanged, and read only workouts edited since the last copy

title: The Charts page reads weekly volume and the training calendar twice on every visit and throws one copy away
what: Each time the Charts page comes into view, the app reads the weekly lifted weight and the day-by-day training shading once inside the main bundle, then reads both again with the newer counting rule and drops the first copies. On a phone with years of workouts this is wasted work on every visit.
expected: Each number on the Charts page is read once per visit.
fix_line: Leave the old weekly volume and calendar reads out of the bundle the Charts page uses

title: The Workout tab reads every workout ever saved just to count them, each time the tab opens
what: Every time the Workout tab comes into view, the 'only on this phone' card fetches the id of every workout on the phone to count them, even for members who are signed in and will never see the card. On a phone with years of workouts this is small wasted work on the busiest screen.
expected: The card asks the phone for a count only, and skips the read for signed-in members.
fix_line: Count workouts with one counting question, and skip it when the member is signed in

title: Opening the app starts about nine background jobs at the same moment as the first screen
what: The moment the app opens it redraws the widgets (working out today's what-to-beat lines from each lift's history when a Today widget is placed), resets reminders, re-sends owed Health Connect workouts, reads weigh-ins, and starts four gym syncs (leaderboard, gym mates, busy machines, trainers), all at once and with no wait. The same widget redraw with the what-to-beat work runs again every time the member leaves the app and comes back. On a cheap phone with a long history this can make the first seconds feel slow. Not measured on a phone.
expected: The first screen comes up first; the background jobs follow a moment later, one after another, and the widget redraw on leaving the app skips work whose answer has not changed.
fix_line: Start the background jobs a few seconds after the first screen shows, one at a time, and skip the widget's what-to-beat work when nothing changed

title: After an app update, the first opening waits for one-time repair jobs before showing anything
what: On the first start after an update, the app finishes several one-time clean-ups (fixing old records, fixing imported workout times, fixing copied routines, adding new library exercises) one after another before the first screen appears. Each one says it never holds up start-up, but each is waited for. On a phone with years of workouts, the record fix rebuilds every affected exercise in turn, so that first opening can sit on the loading screen. Later starts are quick because each job remembers it is done.
expected: The first screen appears straight away; one-time clean-ups run just after it, like the lighter-set record fix already does.
fix_line: Start the one-time clean-ups after the first screen shows, the same way the lighter-set fix is delayed

title: The Body page draws every weigh-in ever logged at once
what: The History list under the body weight or measurement graph shows every entry the member and the gym ever recorded, all drawn in one go, and the whole list is read again each time the page comes back into view. A member who weighs in daily has about 365 rows after a year and over 1,000 after three, so the page gets slower to open and scroll over time. Not timed on a real phone.
expected: The newest entries show first, a page at a time with a Show more button, as the exercise History tab already does.
who: members who log body weight often
how_often: every time the Body page opens, worse each month
fix_line: Show the newest 30 entries and add a Show more button

title: The Progress photos page checks every photo's file on the phone each time it opens, before showing any photo
what: Each time the Progress photos page comes into view, it first runs the after-a-fresh-install repair: it lists the phone's photo backup folder and then, one photo at a time, checks whether each photo's file is still there. Only after that does it read the photo list and draw it. For a member with backup on and a few hundred photos, every visit waits for a few hundred file checks that almost always find nothing to repair.
expected: The repair runs once after a fresh install or a restore, or runs after the photos are already on screen, so opening the page costs the same with 10 photos as with 500.
fix_line: Run the photo repair once after an install or restore, or after the list is shown

title: The phone screen never turns off while a workout is open, and there is no setting to let it sleep
what: While the live workout screen is open, the app keeps the phone screen switched on the whole time, even when the phone sits in a pocket or on the floor between sets. A 75-minute workout keeps the screen lit for 75 minutes. There is no choice in Settings to turn this off, so members who lock their phone between sets cannot.
expected: A Workout setting 'Keep screen on during a workout' (on by default is fine), so members who want to save battery can let the screen sleep; the rest timer already rings with the screen off.
fix_line: Add a Keep screen on switch to Workout settings and follow it

title: Every switch to the Gym tab asks the gym server about seven questions again, even seconds after the last time
what: Each time the member taps into the Gym tab, the app at once asks the gym for its shop list, the member's orders, the gym's name and look, the messages, the workout offer, the reminders and any unsent leave, with no wait between visits. Going back and forth between tabs repeats all of it. On a slow 4G phone this costs data and battery and slows the tab's other answers, though the screen keeps showing what it already had.
expected: Opening the tab again within a few minutes reuses what the phone already has (as the opening hours and diet plans already do), and only a pull to refresh asks for everything at once.
fix_line: Ask the gym again on tab open only when the last ask is a few minutes old; a pull still asks at once

title: Every app opening re-sends up to a year of workouts to the gym's trainers, though the rule says once every 6 hours
what: With sharing with trainers switched on, the app is meant to send on opening at most once every 6 hours. The time of the last send is kept only while the app is running, so each fresh opening counts as 'never sent'. Each time, the phone reads up to a year of sets plus the member's whole older history for best weights, and uploads up to about 280 KB. The gym mates share and the leaderboard push forget their wait the same way. Android closes apps often, so on a slow 4G phone most openings pay for this in data and battery.
expected: The last send time is saved on the phone, so a fresh opening within 6 hours sends nothing; a saved workout still sends at once.
who: members who share with trainers or gym mates
fix_line: Save the time of the last send on the phone so the 6-hour wait survives closing the app

title: Each member who leaves makes the database read the busy-machines records of every gym
what: When a member leaves, a clean-up deletes their busy-machine records by member alone. That list is only indexed by gym first, so the delete reads the list for every gym. Removing a member for good does the same on the record of which gym messages they have seen. The database's own advisor flags both. It is small today and grows with every gym.
expected: Each list has an index on the member, so a leave touches only that member's rows.
who: every gym, as the platform grows
fix_line: Add an index on the member for the busy-machines list and the messages-seen list

title: Choosing a before or after photo loads every progress photo at once
what: When a member taps Before or After to pick another photo, the strip underneath draws every progress photo they have ever taken in one go, each read from the full-size original. With a long photo history this can make the sheet stutter or open slowly on a cheap phone.
expected: The strip only draws the photos on screen (and the next few) as the member scrolls, using small thumbnails.
how_often: each time the photo strip opens
fix_line: Draw the strip as a scrolling list that only shows visible photos

title: Workout photos in the Profile feed are drawn from the full-size camera pictures
what: Workout photos are kept at the camera's full size (only lightly compressed, never made smaller). Each card in the Profile workouts feed shows up to four of them as small squares, and the workout page shows them too, each time opening the full-size picture. Scrolling a feed with many photo workouts on a cheap phone has to decode several large pictures per card, which can make the scroll stutter. Not measured on a phone.
expected: Each photo is saved with a small preview copy, and the feed and the workout page show the preview; the full picture opens only when the member taps to view it full screen.
how_often: every time the feed is scrolled
fix_line: Save a small preview of each workout photo and show that in the feed and on the workout page

title: The Exercises list goes through every set ever logged each time it opens, to show when each exercise was last done
what: Each visit to Profile, Exercises works out 'Last: 12 Oct' for every exercise by grouping every set the member has ever saved and joining each to its workout. After an import of five years (about 32,000 sets) this read grows with the whole history and is not part of the timed speed check.
expected: The last-done day is kept up to date when a workout is saved, or read from a short index, so opening the list costs the same in year five as in week one.
who: members with long or imported history
how_often: every visit to the Exercises list
fix_line: Read the last-done days from a small index or keep them updated on save, and add the list to the speed check

title: The five-years-of-data speed check is never run automatically and has no time limit
what: A speed check that loads a made-up five-year history and times every member action exists, but the normal test run skips it, no cloud workflow runs it, and it only prints times without failing on any. A change that makes the workout screen or History slow with long history would pass every check.
expected: The long-history speed check runs in the cloud on each change and fails when a key action (start a workout, open History, open an exercise) reads far more rows or statements than its recorded budget.
fix_line: Run the long-history speed check in the cloud and fail on a statement or row-count budget

title: Routines and their exercises have no index for which folder or routine they belong to
what: The routine tables are looked up by folder and by routine on every routine open, reorder, move and delete, and deleting a folder or routine clears its exercises through the same link, but none of these links has an index, so each lookup goes through the whole table. The tables are small (tens of routines), so members will not feel it today.
expected: The routine-to-folder and exercise-to-routine links have an index, like the workout and set tables already do.
fix_line: Add the two missing indexes to the start-up index list

title: After every workout, the new-badge line re-reads the member's whole lifting history
what: When a workout is finished, the badge line on the Workout complete screen works out every badge again from scratch: every workout ever saved, every heavy set ever logged, the whole body weight list and all records. The saved copy is thrown away because the history just changed, so this happens on every finish. It does not hold up the screen, but on a long history the badge line can appear late on a slow phone, and the five-years-of-data speed check never times it.
expected: Only the badges this workout could have earned are checked, or the badge read is at least timed in the five-years speed check with a limit.
fix_line: Add the badge read to the five-years speed check; if it is slow, check only what the new workout adds

title: The body map's 'last trained' line and the Statistics 'Main exercises' go through every set ever logged each time they load
what: Each time the Progress page reloads its week, the body map works out when each muscle was last trained by grouping every working set the member has ever saved. The Statistics screen does the same to find the six most-done exercises, counting every workout of every exercise ever. After an import of years of history these reads grow with the whole history, run again on every visit, and are not checked against any time limit. The hidden 'Which muscles are ready' card uses the same whole-history read.
expected: The last-trained day and the times-done count per exercise are kept up to date when a workout is saved (or read from a small summary), so these screens cost the same in year five as in week one.
fix_line: Keep each exercise's last day and workout count up to date when a workout is saved, and read that instead

title: Nothing in the cloud checks how fast the websites and the gym panel load on a phone
what: No automatic run measures page speed or layout jumps. The 10-minute outage alarm only asks whether each site answers. A hand run on 21 Nov found the gym-owner page jumping (0.265, over Google's poor line) and the member home page slow to show (3.0 s); no run would have caught either, and a slower change would ship unnoticed.
expected: A cloud run measures the main pages on a slow 4G phone after each change and warns when a page gets slower or jumps more than a set line.
who: gym owners and members opening the sites
fix_line: Add a cloud page-speed run on the main pages with warning lines for load time and layout jumps

title: No test ever runs a gym with hundreds of members, so slow big lists are never seen
what: The cross-role journeys make their own small fresh gyms, and the database tests only build a few hundred items to test size limits. No run fills a gym with 500 or more members and times the member list, Today, dues or the reports, so a page that crawls for a big gym would pass every check.
expected: One cloud run seeds a test gym with 500 to 2,000 members and a year of history and times the biggest panel pages and lists against a set line.
fix_line: Add a seeded big test gym and time its main pages in a cloud run

title: Phone app start time and the workout screen with a long history are never timed
what: The phone release test checks that screens work, not how long they take. The only run that reports slow starts is the real-phone robot crawl, which never blocks a release and stops green with nothing tested when its keys are missing. So an app that opens in 6 seconds, or a workout screen that lags for a member with years of history, would still be released.
expected: The phone test records the cold start time and the workout screen open time with a long history, and warns when either passes a set line.
fix_line: Time the cold start and a long-history workout screen in the phone test and warn on a set line

title: The watch test checks nothing is left running, but never measures battery use over a workout
what: The watch test on each watch change proves no wake lock is held after a rest and no busy loop runs in a quiet dimmed minute. It never measures how much battery or screen-on time a full workout costs, so a slow drain that is not a stuck lock would pass.
expected: The watch test also records battery use and screen-on time over a set length of workout and warns above a set line.
fix_line: Add a battery and screen-on reading over a timed workout to the watch test

title: The database check never looks for missing indexes, so 23 unindexed links passed and new ones will too
what: The database run checks broken functions at error level, security and feature tests. It never runs the speed advice, so the live database already has 23 links between tables with no index and 5 tables with no main key, and any new one added in a change passes without a word.
expected: The database run fails, or at least warns, when a change adds a table link without an index or a table without a main key.
fix_line: Add a check for unindexed table links and missing main keys to the database run

title: Each check-in, membership look and receipt save reads every membership or payment the gym ever had
what: To find one member's plans, the server goes through all of the gym's memberships, and to work out what a membership still owes on each receipt save it goes through all of the gym's payments. There is no index on which member or which membership a row belongs to, so the work grows with every year of the gym's history. The QR check-in, the member's My membership screen, the gym's workout plans in the app, the branch visitor check and every receipt save all do this. Crispy Curves has 1 membership and 1 payment today, so nobody feels it yet; a 500-member gym after a few years holds thousands of each.
expected: Looking up one member's plans or one membership's payments touches only those rows, however old the gym is.
who: members checking in, owners and desk saving receipts at big old gyms
how_often: every check-in, receipt save and membership screen open
fix_line: Add an index on the member and on the membership inside the gym's memberships and payments.

title: Deleting a gym reads the offer history and the photo-upload passes of every gym
what: The workout-offer history and the short-lived photo-upload passes are linked to their gym, but that link has no index. When HQ deletes a gym, the database has to read these lists for all gyms to find the rows to remove. Both lists are small today, so the cost is tiny; the offer history grows with every offer at every gym.
expected: Every link from a list to its gym has an index, so deleting one gym touches only its own rows.
how_often: each time a gym is deleted
fix_line: Add an index on the gym column of the offer history and the photo-upload passes.

title: Nine links added in the newer database lists have no index, so removing a member, a staff login or a gym reads those lists for every gym
what: Several lists added in this stretch of changes point at a member, a staff login, a gym or a payment record without an index on that link: plan requests and report requests (member), trainer questions (who it was sent to and who answered), the phone pop-up queues, report files and free-trial numbers (gym), and MettleUp payments (ledger line). When the thing they point at is removed, the database has to read the whole list across all gyms to find the matching lines. The database's own advisor flags all nine. Small today; it grows with every gym.
expected: Every link has an index that starts with the linked column, so a removal touches only its own rows.
how_often: each time a member, staff login or gym is removed
fix_line: Add one index on each of the nine links in a small additive change

title: Opening the leaderboard adds up the whole gym's last 30 days about eight times
what: Each time a member opens the leaderboard, the database adds up every member's last 30 days separately for the top 10, again to find the member's own total, and again to count who is ahead, for workouts and then for kg; it also counts the month's members and the challenge hitters the same way. With 500 members that is about 15,000 day lines read eight times per opening, and the owner's view does it again. Nothing keeps the answer between openings.
expected: The 30-day totals are worked out once per opening (or kept for a minute) and the top 10, the member's place and the counts all come from that one result.
who: members of big gyms and their owners
fix_line: Work out the 30-day totals once per call and rank, find and count from that

title: The nightly backup builds the whole database as one answer, so it will stop working once the data gets big
what: The nightly backup reads every table, every row, into one single answer inside the database and sends it in one go. The database has a hard size limit for one such answer (a few hundred MB), and the whole copy must also fit in memory and in one call's time. Workout cloud copies and check-ins grow every day, so at some point the backup will fail every night, and there is no way to take it in pieces.
expected: The backup reads the database in pieces (per table, or per table in pages) so it keeps working however big the data grows, and a test checks a large copy.
who: every gym, if a restore is ever needed
how_often: every night once the data passes the limit
fix_line: Read the backup in pages per table and stream them into the stored parts

title: The desk's plan request list reads every request the gym ever had
what: The desk's list of pause and renew requests asks for pending ones or ones decided in the last 14 days. The decided time has no index, so the database reads every request the gym ever had each time the list loads, and the index made for this list is never used (the advisor says so). It grows with every request, year after year.
expected: The list uses an index on status and decided time, so it reads only pending and recent requests.
how_often: each time the requests list loads
fix_line: Add an index on gym, status and decided time, or split the read into pending plus recent

title: Seven more links added in the newer lists have no index, so removing a staff login or a gym reads those lists for every gym
what: Lists added in this stretch of changes point at a staff login, a gym or a payment record with no index on that link: personal-training bookings, browser alert sign-ups, member message threads (the chosen trainer) and message lines (the gym and the staff who wrote them), plus the plan payment links and the booked plan changes (payment record). When a staff login, a gym or a payment record is removed, the database reads the whole list across all gyms to find the matching lines. Message lines grow fastest, with every message at every gym. The database's own advisor flags all seven. Small today.
expected: Every link has an index that starts with the linked column, so a removal touches only its own rows.
how_often: each time a staff login, gym or payment record is removed
fix_line: Add one index on each of the seven links in a small additive change

title: The owner's list of direct reads of their gym goes through the whole two-year record, and the gym index made for it is never used
what: When an owner opens the record of direct reads of their gym's data, the database walks the record of every direct read for all gyms, newest first, until it finds 100 that name this gym or no gym. The search is written in a way the gym index cannot help with, so the advisor says that index has never been used. For a gym that is rarely named, each opening reads up to two years of everyone's entries.
expected: The owner's list uses the gym index and reads only the entries that name this gym, plus the few that name none.
who: gym owners checking who read their data
how_often: each time the record is opened
fix_line: Write the gym filter as an array-contains test so the gym index is used, and add the no-gym entries separately

title: A gym message to a big gym reaches members' phones only about 30 a minute, and a busy hour can drop pop-ups
what: Phone pop-ups go out one phone per call, and each one-minute run may make about 45 calls in all. The fee and payment feeds, the direct-read record and the admin-app alerts spend part of that first (the admin-app alerts alone up to 12), so about 30 phones get the pop-up each minute. A message to a gym with 500 members takes around a quarter of an hour to reach everyone. If several big gyms send at the same time, the queue can run past 6 hours, and then the server skips the rest, so those members never get the pop-up.
expected: A message to a 500-member gym reaches every phone within a minute or two, and no pop-up is dropped because the queue was long.
who: members of big gyms, and their owners
how_often: every message or offer sent to a gym with more than about 30 phones
fix_line: Send pop-ups to many phones in one call (Firebase topics or batch sending), or move the sender to a plan with more calls per run

title: Every minute, the online-payment alert reads every online payment any gym ever got
what: Once a minute, the job that tells a gym 'Asha paid online' looks for payments from the last 15 minutes. No list is sorted by the time paid, so the database goes through every paid online request of every gym, ever. Payment requests are never removed. The fee-request job does the same with every open request. Cloudflare's small database has a free limit of reads per day: with about 3,500 online payments stored, this one job alone uses the whole day's free reads (1,440 runs a day). After that, the reads either cost money or stop, along with the gym alerts.
expected: Each minute's check reads only the last few minutes of payments, however many have been stored.
who: gyms with online payments switched on, and MettleUp's running cost
how_often: every minute, getting worse with each payment
fix_line: Add a list sorted by status and time paid (and by status and time created) for these two checks, and remove old payment requests after a set time

title: The 10-minute payment check reads every old payment link of every gym, and old links are never removed
what: Every 10 minutes the server looks for payment links to check. Its search can only narrow by the link's state, so it reads every open, cancelled and expired link ever made, for all gyms, then sorts them, to pick 40. A second step reads every link of a payment company for each disconnected gym. Payment links are never deleted, so this work and the database bill grow with every link, 144 times a day.
expected: The check reads only the links still inside the checking window, using a lookup made for that, and links past the window are tidied away or kept out of the search.
who: MettleUp (server cost and speed once online payments are on)
how_often: every 10 minutes, growing with every payment link
fix_line: Add a lookup on the link's date and state for the 10-minute check, and remove or archive links long past their window

title: Each feedback or help message reads the whole feedback table to check the daily limit
what: Before saving a feedback or help question, the server counts the last day's messages. The count has no lookup by time that it can use, so it reads every stored message and crash report (kept up to a year) each time someone writes in.
expected: The daily-limit count reads only the last day's messages through a lookup on the time.
who: MettleUp (server cost); members and owners wait a little longer as messages pile up
fix_line: Add a lookup on the message time and use it for the daily-limit count

title: The dimmed watch keeps its processor awake for every whole rest
what: When the watch's own dim state is on (Always-on display on) and a rest runs, the app holds the processor awake for the whole rest, plus 5 seconds, so the dim countdown can change every second. In a workout that is mostly rests, the processor stays awake for most of the workout, while the watch would normally sleep and redraw the dim screen once a minute. This was chosen on purpose so the dim countdown shows real seconds. The cost to the battery was never measured.
expected: The battery cost of a one-second dim countdown is measured on a real watch over a full workout. If it is high, the dim screen redraws less often (for example every 10 s, then every second for the last 10 s).
who: members with a watch and Always-on display on
fix_line: Measure the battery cost over a full workout. If it is high, redraw the dim countdown less often until the last seconds

title: The bright rest screen redraws 4 to 5 times a second although its numbers change once a second
what: On the bright screen, the rest countdown wakes up every 0.2 s and the Rest is over count-up every 0.25 s, so the screen is redrawn 4 to 5 times for each change of the seconds shown. On the app's own dim screen, the same loop already waits for the next whole second. The extra redraws cost a little battery on every rest the member looks at.
expected: The bright countdown and count-up wake once per shown second, in step with the digits, as the dim screen already does.
how_often: every rest while the screen is bright
fix_line: Wait for the next whole second on the bright screen too, as the dim screen already does

title: The gym-owner website jumps around while it loads on a phone
what: On a mid-range phone over slow 4G, Google's speed test scores the gym-owner site's layout movement at 0.265, worse than Google's 'poor' line of 0.25, and it is the lowest-scoring public page (86). The page loads three web fonts in ten weights that swap in after the text is drawn, and the live workout scene at the top changes its text and numbers as soon as it comes on screen, so words and blocks move under the reader's thumb.
expected: The page stays still while it loads (layout movement under 0.1), so an owner can start reading and tapping straight away.
how_often: every first visit on a phone
fix_line: Find the parts that move in the speed report, give them fixed room, and load fewer font weights with matching fallback sizes.

title: The member website's main picture takes 3 seconds to show on slow 4G
what: Google's speed test on a mid-range phone over slow 4G shows the main picture of the member site after 3.0 seconds, above Google's 2.5-second 'good' line. The page first waits for three web font families (including the Hindi one, also for English readers), and the main phone picture is not marked as the first thing to fetch.
expected: The main picture shows within 2.5 seconds on a slow Indian 4G phone.
how_often: every first visit on a phone
fix_line: Mark the main phone picture to load first and trim the font list so it does not hold up the page.

title: The gym invite page shifts after it opens and is the heaviest public page
what: The invite link page a gym shares (/j/ code) moves after it is drawn: the gym's logo is swapped in only once it has downloaded, and the 'Become a member' card appears only after a second question to the server comes back. Google's speed test measures the movement at 0.109, just above the 0.1 'good' line, and the page weighs 491 KiB, the most of all public pages, mostly the gym's full-size logo shown in a small box.
expected: The page keeps room for the logo and the member card from the start, and downloads a logo no bigger than the box shows.
who: new members opening a gym's invite link
fix_line: Reserve space for the late parts of the invite page and serve a small copy of the gym logo.

title: Each visit to a gym's web page asks again whether the gym takes online payment
what: The gym's page details are kept at the edge for a while, but once online joining payment is switched on, every single page view runs the 'can this gym be paid online' check again, with several database reads, before the page is sent. A gym page shared widely will do this work for every visitor, slowing each page and using up the free plan's read allowance.
expected: The online-payment answer is kept for a short time like the rest of the page, so a busy page does not repeat the same reads for every visitor.
how_often: every view while online payment is on
fix_line: Keep the online-payment answer with the cached page details for a minute or so.

title: The Cloudflare free-limit warning comes once a week, after the busy day has passed
what: HQ looks at Cloudflare's daily request count only on Monday night, for the week before. A day that runs past the free daily limit on a Tuesday stops every MettleUp app until 05:30, and HQ only says so the next Monday. Only requests are watched; other free Cloudflare limits are not.
expected: A warning on Needs you the same day the count passes 60%, early enough to switch to the paid plan before every app stops.
how_often: on any day the apps get unusually busy
fix_line: Check the day's count every few hours and warn the same day; or move to the paid plan once gyms rely on it

title: Gym server storage has no warning on Needs you, and its limit is a fixed number
what: The System page shows gym server storage against a fixed 500 MB and turns the bar red past 80%, but nothing ever reaches Needs you, so it is only seen if he opens System. The 500 MB is typed in, whatever plan the project is really on, and the page does not say what happens when it is full (the database stops taking new records).
expected: A Needs you line at 70% and 90% of the real plan limit, saying what stops when it is full.
how_often: once storage grows near the limit
fix_line: Add a storage line to Needs you and read the limit from the plan instead of a fixed number

title: Picture storage, download traffic and code-store storage are not watched anywhere in HQ
what: The System page shows only database size and Cloudflare requests. Picture storage (free limit 1 GB), download traffic from the gym server, and the build files kept in the code store (about 401 GB today) are not shown and have no warning. Nobody knows how close they are until a service stops or bills.
expected: One line each on the System page with the use against the limit, and a Needs you line near each limit.
how_often: once any of these grows near its limit
fix_line: Add picture storage, traffic and build-file storage to the System page with a warning near each limit

title: The System page's AI cost this month leaves out the AI Assistant and the English helper
what: 'AI reads this month' on the System page counts only the column-matching AI. The AI Assistant's cost (the most expensive model) and the English helper's cost are left out, so the month's AI bill shown is too low. There is no warning when the month's AI spend passes an amount, and no ceiling for all gyms together.
expected: One AI total for the month covering every AI use, with a warning on Needs you past a set amount.
how_often: every month once the AI Assistant is used
fix_line: Add the Assistant and English helper costs to the month's total and warn past a set amount

title: The trial gyms' shared AI money pool runs out with no warning to MettleUp first
what: All trial and unpaid gyms share one small monthly AI money pool (15 dollars unless changed). Each trial gym may ask 20 questions a day, so a modest number of ordinary trial gyms can use it up before the month ends. Nothing warns MettleUp as the pool fills; when it is used up the server writes one log line and every trial gym is told the AI Assistant is resting till next month. MettleUp learns of it only when an owner complains.
expected: A warning to MettleUp (on HQ Needs you) when the pool passes about 70% and again at 90%, early enough to raise it before trial gyms are turned away.
who: owners of trial gyms, and MettleUp
how_often: any month with more than a handful of active trial gyms
fix_line: Warn MettleUp in HQ as the trial pool fills, and show the pool's level on the System page

title: A paying gym is handled as a trial gym whenever its paid check fails
what: Before each question the server asks whether the gym has paid. If that check cannot be read (gym server slow or down, an odd answer), the paying gym is treated as a trial gym: it gets the smaller 20-a-day allowance, its use is added to the trial gyms' shared money pool, and if that pool is used up it is told the AI Assistant is resting till next month. The owner decided paying gyms are never stopped by a money cap.
expected: A paying gym keeps its own allowance and is never refused by the trial money pool because one check failed; an unreadable check is retried or the last known answer is used.
how_often: when the gym server is slow or down
fix_line: Remember the gym's last known paid answer and use it when the check fails

title: When all gyms together reach the day's speaking ceiling, the owner is told he used up his own time
what: Speaking a request has two daily limits: 10 minutes per gym and 10 hours for all gyms together. Both give the same answer: You have used today's speaking time. An owner who has not spoken at all that day reads that he used his time, when in fact other gyms used the shared ceiling.
expected: At the shared ceiling the owner reads that speaking is busy for today and he can type instead, not that he used his own time.
how_often: on days when many gyms speak requests
fix_line: Tell apart the two limits and give the shared one its own words

title: A spoken request that could not be turned into words still uses up speaking time
what: The clip's seconds are taken from the day's speaking time before the speech service is asked. If every speech service fails, the owner is told to try again or type, but the seconds are not given back. Typed questions that fail are given back; spoken ones are not.
expected: Seconds of a clip that could not be turned into words are given back, as failed typed questions are.
how_often: when the speech service is down
fix_line: Give the seconds back when no speech service answered

title: The paid WhatsApp code limit gives no warning before it is reached
what: When the older 'we send you a code' way is on, every code is a paid WhatsApp message. There is a cap of 200 a day for everyone. Nobody is warned as it gets close. When it is reached, the only sign is one line in the server log, and code sign-up and Forgot PIN quietly vanish from the panel until midnight.
expected: MettleUp gets a warning on Needs you or by message at about 80% of the day's cap, and again when sending stops, with the count for the day.
who: MettleUp, and owners who forgot their PIN
how_often: only while the send-a-code way is switched on and a busy day passes 200 codes
fix_line: Raise an alert to MettleUp at 80% and at 100% of the day's code cap

title: A full device throws away the desk's offline copy of the gym with no word to the desk
what: Each time the panel updates the copy of the gym kept for no-internet days, it first deletes the old copy, then writes the new one. When the device is out of space the write fails, so the device is left with no copy at all. Only a hidden log line notes it. The next time the internet drops, the panel cannot open members or dues, though the desk believed it could.
expected: The old copy stays until the new one is safely written (one step), and the desk sees a warning that this device can no longer work offline.
how_often: whenever the desk device's storage is full
fix_line: Replace the copy in one step and tell the desk when it could not be kept

title: Payments waiting to be sent can be wiped by the browser when the device runs low on space
what: Payments, check-ins and new members taken with no internet wait in the browser's own store. The panel never asks the browser to keep that store for good and never checks how much space is left. Under low space a browser may clear a site's store, taking unsent receipts with it, and the desk gets no warning beforehand.
expected: The panel asks the browser to keep its store, checks free space, and warns the desk early when space is low while anything is waiting to be sent.
how_often: rarely: low disk on the desk device while offline items wait
fix_line: Ask the browser to keep the store and warn when space is low

title: A gym kept only in this browser hits its space limit with no early warning
what: A gym kept only in the browser has about 5 MB. The panel says 'This browser is full' only when a save already failed, maybe in the middle of taking a payment. Backup copies of unreadable data are kept for ever in the same space and are never cleared.
expected: A warning when the browser gym is about 80% full, pointing to 'put your records online', and old backups cleared after they were downloaded or after a time.
how_often: once a browser-only gym has years of records
fix_line: Warn early when the browser gym is nearly full and clear old backups

title: If the gym server's storage limit is reached, every desk only sees 'Something went wrong'
what: When the gym server reaches its plan's storage limit it stops taking new records. The panel has no words for this: every save at every gym shows 'Something went wrong. Please try again.', so staff keep retrying and owners cannot tell it is not their fault. Unsent offline items do stay kept.
expected: A clear message that MettleUp is having a problem and the records are kept and will go later, plus an alert to MettleUp.
how_often: only if the database reaches its plan limit (about 18 MB of 500 MB now)
fix_line: Show a plain 'MettleUp problem, your records are kept' message for server-full errors

title: When the picture store is full, a gym owner is told the logo is over 1 MB
what: The logo upload turns any failure whose message holds words like 'exceeded' or 'size' into 'That logo is over 1 MB. Pick a smaller one.' The logo is already shrunk and checked to be under 1 MB before upload, so the likely cause of such a failure is the picture store's plan limit, not the file. The owner keeps trying smaller logos that can never work, and nobody at MettleUp is told.
expected: A failure from a full picture store tells the owner it is our problem and to message MettleUp, and MettleUp gets a warning before the store fills up.
how_often: only once the picture store reaches its plan limit
fix_line: Tell a storage-full failure apart from a too-big file and show plain words that point to MettleUp

title: Member photos are kept inside the main gym database with no cap per gym, so they eat the free 500 MB limit that every gym shares
what: Each photo taken on Add member is saved as a picture of up to 100 KB (about 60 KB aimed) inside the same database that holds every gym's members and receipts. There is no limit on how many photos one gym keeps, and photos of deleted members stay behind. About 8,000 photos across all gyms would fill the free 500 MB on their own. When the database is full, saving members and payments can stop for every gym at once. Every screen that shows faces also pulls the photos through the database, which uses the free download traffic.
expected: Photos live somewhere whose size does not risk the main database (or each gym has a photo cap), old photos are cleared, and MettleUp sees how much space photos take before the limit.
who: all gyms, owners and front desk
how_often: grows with every photo; risk once many gyms use photos
fix_line: Track photo space in HQ, set a per-gym photo cap, clear photos of removed members, and plan a move to file storage before the limit

title: Nobody at MettleUp is warned when AI column matching nears or hits its daily ceiling
what: AI column matching in the member import allows 20 reads a gym and 1,000 for all gyms together each India day. When a gym or all gyms reach the ceiling the server quietly refuses without even a log line, and HQ only lists past use per gym. There is no warning as the shared ceiling gets close, so on a busy import day every owner silently falls back to matching by hand and MettleUp does not find out.
expected: HQ warns when the shared daily ceiling passes about 80 percent, and each time a gym or all gyms hit the ceiling it is counted and shown so the limit can be raised.
how_often: on days with many imports, or after abuse
fix_line: Count refusals at the ceiling and show a warning in HQ before and when the daily ceiling is reached

title: An owner who used up today's AI matches is only told the AI was not available
what: The server answers with a clear reason when today's AI matches are used up, but the import screen shows the same line for every failure: matched without AI because it was not available. The owner does not learn that it will work again tomorrow, and may re-upload the file hoping for AI.
expected: When the day's limit is the reason, the line says today's AI matches are used up and they come back tomorrow.
how_often: each import after the day's limit
fix_line: Show a separate line for the daily-limit case

title: Each admin panel on screen asks the server every minute, so under a hundred busy gyms can use up the free daily request limit for everyone
what: While the admin panel is in view, the Needs you check asks the server once a minute, and reads its other lists every five minutes. A desk that keeps the panel open through a 16-hour day makes over a thousand requests. The free Cloudflare plan allows 100,000 a day for all gyms together, so roughly 80 to 90 such desks fill it, and then every gym panel and member app stops answering until the day resets.
expected: The repeating checks stay well inside the shared daily limit as gyms grow, or the plan is moved before the limit is near, and what happens at the limit is written down.
how_often: every day once about 80 desks keep the panel open
fix_line: Slow the minute check or push alerts to the panel instead, and decide the plan move before growth reaches the limit

title: A web-page chat question stopped by a limit does not say whether the day ran out or the AI credits did
what: When a visitor question on the gym web page was not sent to the AI, the owner sees one note that says a daily limit or no AI credits left. The owner cannot tell whether to wait for tomorrow or buy credits.
expected: The note names which limit stopped it and what the owner can do about it.
how_often: each time a limit is hit
fix_line: Give the two cases their own note, with the next step for each

title: Each door machine calls in every 30 seconds, and nothing watches what that adds up to
what: A door machine is told to check in every 30 seconds, all day and night. That is about 2,900 calls a day per machine to MettleUp's door service, and each call makes up to three calls to the gym server. Cloudflare's free plan allows 100,000 calls a day for the whole account, so about 30 machines would use it up on their own, before any desk or member traffic. Nothing counts the door service calls and nobody at MettleUp is warned as they climb. Once the allowance runs out, machines get an error, keep their punches, and no member visits show at any gym until the next day. Not live today: the door service is written but not switched on.
expected: Machines check in no more often than needed, door service calls are counted with the rest, and MettleUp is warned well before the daily allowance runs out.
who: owners and members of gyms with door machines
how_often: every day once enough machines are added
fix_line: Make machines check in less often, count door service calls, and warn MettleUp before the daily limit

title: Anyone can call the door service with made-up machine numbers as often as they like
what: The door service answers any caller, and each call with an unknown machine number writes to the gym server. Nothing limits how often one sender may call. Someone sending made-up numbers in a loop would use up the free daily call allowance for every gym, and also push out the list of 'machines we can see calling' (it keeps only 5,000), so a real owner adding a new machine would no longer be told it was seen. Not live today.
expected: Calls from unknown machines are limited per sender, and the 'seen calling' list cannot be flooded out.
who: all gyms; owners adding a machine
fix_line: Limit calls per sender and per unknown machine number before writing anything

title: A machine with a big backlog of punches may be refused again and again
what: The gym server refuses any single upload with more than 5,000 punches, and the door service cuts any upload larger than 2 MB. A machine that was offline for weeks, or a busy gym's machine, may send more than that at once. The refusal comes back as an error, the machine keeps the same punches and tries the same upload again 30 seconds later, so it can stay stuck and send nothing new. If the upload is cut at 2 MB instead, the punches past the cut may be lost without a word. How big a machine's uploads get depends on the machine model and is not known.
expected: A large catch-up upload is saved in parts, or the machine is told to send smaller batches, and the owner is told when a machine is stuck.
who: gyms whose machine was offline a long time
fix_line: Save large uploads in parts and warn the owner when a machine keeps failing

title: An open payment link asks the server every 4 seconds for as long as the screen stays open
what: While a payment link is on the desk screen, the app asks the server every 4 seconds whether it has been paid. It keeps asking when the tab is in the background or the desk has walked away, until the link is paid, cancelled or runs out, and links last for days. One screen left open overnight makes about 20,000 calls a day, all counted against the same free daily allowance every gym shares.
expected: The app slows down after the first few minutes, stops asking while the tab is hidden, and relies on the payment company telling the server when money comes in.
who: gyms using online payments; every gym through the shared allowance
how_often: whenever a payment screen is left open
fix_line: Slow the checks down over time and pause them while the screen is hidden

title: Each 'Well done' sent from Training progress uses one of the gym's 10 member messages a day, with no warning
what: Every 'Well done' or 'How's it going' sent from the Training progress page counts as a full member message. The gym can send only 10 a day. An owner who cheers 10 members has used up the day, and a later 'gym closed today' notice is refused. The Training progress page never says that cheers use the daily limit or how many are left.
expected: Cheers to one member do not eat the gym's daily notice limit, or the page shows how many messages are left today before the owner sends one.
how_often: on busy days when the owner cheers many members
fix_line: Give one-to-one cheers their own allowance, or show the messages left today on the Training progress page

title: Old product photos are never removed from the picture store
what: When an owner changes a product photo, deletes a product, or a gym is deleted, the old photo file stays in the public picture store for good. Only the product's link to it changes. Every replaced or abandoned photo keeps using the free 1 GB picture store and download traffic.
expected: A replaced or deleted product photo, and the photos of a deleted gym, are removed from the picture store (at once or by a nightly clean-up).
who: MettleUp (cost), every gym sharing the store
how_often: every photo change or product delete
fix_line: Delete the old file when a photo is replaced or a product or gym goes, and clean up files no product points at every night

title: Anyone can start demo gyms and upload photos with no total limit
what: Starting a demo gym needs no sign-in and gives an owner key; up to 300 new gyms an hour are allowed across the whole project, each with a ready-made shop. Each gym can hold 50 upload tickets at once, and one ticket lets in any number of 3 MB photos for 15 minutes. Nothing limits how much one gym stores in total, and demo gyms are never cleared unless their name starts with 'QA '. One person could fill the shared free database and picture store for every real gym.
expected: A cap on photos and space per gym, a one-file-per-ticket rule, a tighter limit on demo gyms per visitor, and unused demo gyms cleared after some days.
fix_line: Limit files per ticket and space per gym, slow down demo starts per visitor, and clear old untouched demo gyms nightly

title: MettleUp's notices in the bell vanish exactly when the server is over its limit
what: The bell asks for MettleUp's notices every 15 minutes and on every Refresh. When that ask fails, for example because the shared daily request limit is used up, the answer is treated as 'no notices' and the notices already on screen are wiped. So a notice like 'we are having trouble today, please wait' disappears from every gym at the very moment it is needed, with no sign that anything failed.
expected: A failed ask keeps the last notices on screen, and the owner can tell MettleUp's messages could not be reached.
how_often: whenever the server is over a limit or down
fix_line: Keep the last notices when the read fails instead of treating a failure as an empty list

title: One member account may store about twice the whole free database in its workout copy
what: Anyone who signs in with Google gets a server copy that is capped only by row count (30,000) and by size per row (32 KB). Together that is close to 1 GB for a single account, while the whole free database is 500 MB and is shared with every gym. Nothing caps the total bytes per member or how fast one account may write. One damaged or misused phone could fill the database and stop every gym's desk from saving.
expected: Each member's copy has a total size cap sized to the plan (a few MB is years of real training) and a pace limit, so one account can never fill the shared database.
who: every gym, through any one member account
fix_line: Add a total size cap per member copy and a write pace limit on the server

title: A very long workout is silently left out of the saved copy while Settings says everything is saved
what: A workout or other item bigger than the copy's size limit per item is skipped and only noted in the developer log. It never joins the waiting count, so the backup line in Settings says the workouts are saved. On a new phone that workout is missing.
expected: The member is told that one workout could not be saved to the account, and it is shown as not saved, or it is split so it fits.
fix_line: Show a not-saved line for items over the size limit, or split them

title: No early warning before a member's saved copy is full
what: The member only hears about the copy limit once it is reached and new workouts stop being saved. Neither the member nor MettleUp gets a warning as the copy gets close to the limit.
expected: A gentle note to the member, and a count for MettleUp, when a copy passes about 80% of its limit.
fix_line: Warn at about 80% full, and list near-full copies in HQ

title: A member learns the phone is out of space only after a workout save has already failed
what: The app has one line for a full phone: 'Couldn't save, your phone's storage may be full', shown only once a save has failed. Nothing checks free space beforehand, so a member in the middle of a workout finds out too late, and until they free space the sets they log are not stored on the phone.
expected: A quiet early note when the phone's free space gets low, before saving starts to fail.
how_often: rarely: only when the phone's storage runs out
fix_line: Check free space at app start and show a calm early note when it is low

title: Nobody is warned before the help box AI answers stop for the month
what: Quick AI answers to help questions are paid from a monthly ceiling of 80 dollars. When the ceiling is reached the answers just stop for every member until the next month. The only trace is a line in the server log. Nothing tells MettleUp it is getting close or has been reached.
expected: A warning to MettleUp at about 80 percent of the monthly ceiling and again when it is reached, so the team can raise it or answer questions by hand.
how_often: once the monthly ceiling is reached
fix_line: Send the team a warning when the monthly AI help spend passes 80 percent and when it hits the ceiling

title: When all members together reach the day's speaking limit, each member is told he spoke too much, and nobody at MettleUp is warned
what: Turning spoken feedback into text has a daily limit of 1,000 clips for everyone together, plus 20 per phone. When the shared limit is reached, a member who has not spoken at all today reads "You have spoken a lot today". No count of clips is shown to the team, and no warning goes out before or at the limit.
expected: A member who hit the shared limit reads that speaking is busy today and can type instead. The team gets a warning near and at the shared daily limit.
how_often: on busy days once the shared limit is reached
fix_line: Tell apart the shared limit from the per-phone one in the words, and warn the team near and at the shared limit

title: Once 1,000 help messages arrive in a day, every member's message is refused and nobody at MettleUp is warned
what: The help and feedback box takes at most 1,000 messages a day from everyone together. After that every member who writes in, even about a real problem, reads "Too many messages today" and the message is not saved. There is no warning to the team before or when this happens.
expected: The team is warned well before the shared daily limit, and a message over the limit is kept on the phone and sent again later instead of being lost.
how_often: on any day the shared limit is reached, including from spam
fix_line: Warn the team near the shared daily limit and let the phone keep and resend a refused message
Ask MettleUp's own server for the newest version first, and wait a few hours after a refusal
title: Members who installed the app from GitHub may never hear of a new version when GitHub's free hourly limit is used up
how_often: when many phones share one internet address
expected: The version check should come from MettleUp's own server (as What's new already does), or wait before asking GitHub again after a refusal. MettleUp should see how often the check is refused.
what: The app asks GitHub's public service, without any sign-in, whether a newer version exists. That free service allows about 60 questions an hour for each internet address. Phones on the same gym wifi or the same mobile network address share that allowance. When it is used up, the app quietly shows no update, records nothing, and asks again on the next check with no waiting. Nobody at MettleUp is told. The What's new lines already moved to MettleUp's own server for a similar GitHub problem, but the version check did not.

title: The phone number check keeps asking the server every 3 seconds even after it has run out of time
what: After a member taps Check with WhatsApp, the app asks MettleUp every 3 seconds whether the message arrived. When the answer is that the check ran out of time, the number was wrong or too many messages came, the app shows the words but keeps asking every 3 seconds for as long as that screen stays open. A phone left on that screen makes about 1,200 calls an hour, all counted against the free daily request allowance that every gym and member shares.
expected: The asking stops as soon as the check has ended, and it slows down after the first few minutes of waiting.
who: every gym and member through the shared allowance
how_often: whenever a member leaves the screen open after a check ends
fix_line: Stop asking once the check has ended, and ask less often the longer it waits

title: My orders asks the gym server every 10 seconds even when no order is waiting
what: While My orders is open, the app asks the database for the full order list every 10 seconds, with no end, even when every order is already collected or cancelled. Each ask adds to the shared free download traffic, and nothing at MettleUp watches that traffic.
expected: Ask often only while an order is still Ordered or Ready, slow down or stop otherwise, and have the traffic counted against the free limit somewhere MettleUp looks.
how_often: every 10 seconds per open My orders page
fix_line: Only keep asking while an order is open, and back off after a few minutes

title: Each visit to the Gym tab reloads the shop list, the orders and the gym with no pause
what: Every time a member comes back to the Gym tab, the app asks the database again for the product list, the order list and the gym itself, even if it asked a few seconds ago. Diet plans and hours wait 10 minutes between asks, but these three do not. Members who switch tabs often multiply the shared free traffic.
expected: The shop list, orders and gym check wait a few minutes between automatic asks, like the hours and diet plans do; a pull still asks at once.
fix_line: Give the automatic shop, orders and gym asks the same 10-minute pause the hours use

title: Each member who shares with trainers keeps up to a year of workouts in the shared free database, with no total budget
what: With sharing with trainers on (the default), the phone sends up to 12 months of workouts, up to about 280 KB, and the server keeps one copy per member of up to 300 KB (a heavy year is about 165 KB). The copy is rewritten after every saved workout. Nothing caps the total across all members, and nothing warns before this table eats into the 500 MB free database that every gym's desk also needs. A few thousand keen members would fill it on their own.
expected: The shared year is sized against the plan (a short summary per workout, or kept outside the main database), there is a total budget, and MettleUp is warned well before the database fills.
fix_line: Send a smaller year, set a total budget for shared workouts, and add an early warning on database size

title: Workout reports of up to 3 MB each are stored in the shared database with no total cap per gym
what: When the desk asks, the phone sends the member's whole workout history as a spreadsheet of up to 3 MB, and the server stores it inside the main database. The desk may ask the same member 5 times a day. Old reports are meant to go after 30 days, but they are only cleared when someone opens that member's reports again. Nothing caps the total per gym, and nothing warns before this fills the 500 MB free database.
expected: Reports live in file storage or are kept small, each gym has a total cap, old reports are cleared on a schedule, and MettleUp is warned before the database fills.
how_often: each time a desk asks for a report
fix_line: Keep report files out of the main database, cap the total per gym and clear old ones on a timer

title: My orders asks the server every 10 seconds even when no order is waiting or the server keeps failing
what: While the My orders page is on screen, the app asks the gym's server for the member's orders every 10 seconds. It keeps doing this when every order is already collected or cancelled, and it does not slow down when the server fails or is over its limit. A phone left on that page makes about 360 calls an hour against the shared free allowance.
expected: The page asks often only while an order is still being prepared, and it slows down after errors.
fix_line: Only ask every 10 seconds while an order is open, and wait longer after a failure

title: Downloaded exercise clips are never cleared, so the phone's space use grows with every exercise opened
what: Each demo clip (about 570 KB with its still frame) is kept on the phone for good once an exercise is opened. Old files are removed only when a newer version of that same clip arrives. There is no size cap, no clear-out of clips not opened for months, and no way for the member to clear them. Today only 2 clips are approved, but the plan is a clip for each of about 400 exercises, which would be over 200 MB kept forever on a phone that opened them all. The files sit in the app's own folder, so the phone does not clear them when space runs low.
expected: The clip folder has a size cap (for example the most recently opened clips only), or old clips are cleared after a while, or the member can clear them in settings.
who: members on phones with little space
how_often: grows over time as more clips are approved
fix_line: Cap the clip folder size and drop the clips opened least recently

title: When a member's workout data alone grows past Android's 25 MB backup limit, the phone's backup silently stops and nobody is told
what: Android's own phone backup holds at most 25 MB per app and backs up nothing at all above that, workouts included. The app already measures the size of the workout data, but only uses it to decide how many photos fit. If the workout data itself passes the limit (years of training or a big import), photos simply get no room and the whole backup quietly stops. No message tells the member that their workouts are no longer saved to their Google account.
expected: Before the workout data nears the 25 MB limit, the member sees a plain warning (for example on the backup card) and is pointed to Save my history or the cloud copy, so they never think they are backed up when they are not.
fix_line: Check the workout data size against the backup limit and show a warning on the backup card well before it is reached

title: Cloud test runs keep about 401 GB of build files, free only while the code stays public
what: Every push to any branch saves a full built copy of the admin app plus test pictures, and each app release saves its install files for the default 90 days because no keep time is set. About 4,100 saved files add up to roughly 401 GB today, over 200 GB of it admin app copies. This costs nothing only because the code store is public. If it is ever made private, use is about 800 times the free 500 MB, cloud runs stop or start billing, and nothing warns beforehand.
expected: Save the built admin app only where it is deployed from (the main branch), set a short keep time on every saved file including release builds, and add a size check with a warning well before any limit.
fix_line: Keep the admin app build only from the main branch, give every saved file a short keep time, and warn on total size

title: One gym can fill the shared database through record saving, with no total limit or speed limit
what: Each save of gym records may carry up to 1,000 records of up to 20 KB each, about 20 MB in one go. Nothing limits how often a gym saves, and nothing limits how much one gym keeps in total. Removed records also stay on the server. Any owner key may do this, including the key a demo gym gets with no sign-up. A broken device or a misuser could fill the free 500 MB database that every gym shares, and then every desk stops saving.
expected: Each gym has a total size budget and a limit on saves per minute, with a warning to MettleUp as a gym nears its budget.
fix_line: Give each gym a size budget and a save speed limit, and warn MettleUp before a gym reaches it

title: Receipt change history and old sign-ins are never cleared, so they grow for ever
what: Every change to a receipt keeps two full copies of it, before and after, with no time limit and no cap per gym. A device that saves all its receipts again adds a pair for each one. Ended and old panel sign-ins are also kept for good. The nightly clean-up removes old access logs, support rows and audit rows, but not these. Both keep eating the shared free database.
